pages.title: Liberal perspective: influences and schools begin
pages.summary: Liberalism offers prescriptions for peace, influenced by Locke's enlightened view of human nature, Kant's Perpetual Peace (free trade, republicanism), Cobden (keep politicians out), Norman Angell's The Great Illusion (war does not benefit even victors) and Wilson's 14 points. Its schools begin with liberal institutionalism (Wilson, Nye) and sociological liberalism (Karl Deutsch).

pages.title: Liberal institutionalism: proposal and advantages
pages.summary: The remaining schools are functionalism (Mitrany, Haas), democratic peace (Doyle), interdependence (Friedman, Rosecrance) and complex interdependence (Keohane, Nye). Liberal institutionalism proposes institutions to contain anarchy, giving a platform for dialogue and making it hard to defect from promises, and institutions have multiplied since the Cold War.

pages.title: Liberal institutionalism: performance and problems
pages.summary: The UN, ASEAN, WHO and BRICS have established rule of law in limited senses, and Hedley Bull sees institutions moving politics from anarchy to anarchical society, yet self-help remains. Problems include narrow national interest, lack of representativeness, transparency, funds, mandate and expertise, and India's experience on Kashmir; Joseph Nogee says nations prefer quasi-negotiations to avoid blame.

pages.title: Sociological liberalism: Rosenau and Burton
pages.summary: Since states have their own compulsions, sociological liberalism moves from Track 1 to Track 2, from communication between states to communication between societies, as world order becomes society-centric. Rosenau notes multiple identities and loyalties, and John Burton's cobweb model, against Wolfers' billiard ball model, shows the state is not the only gateway.

pages.title: Karl Deutsch's security community
pages.summary: Deutsch's security community is an alternative to security dilemma, with members such as Western Europe and North America and ASEAN declaring itself a community in 2015. It emerges through communication, measured by travel, letters and phone calls, so he suggests visa liberalisation and people-to-people contacts, including between India and Pakistan.

pages.title: Security community prospects in South Asia
pages.summary: Success of people-to-people contact between India and Pakistan is uncertain because of vested interests in both countries. South Asia was one of the first places where the concept was applied, for example with Nepal and Bhutan, though it did not strengthen relations with Nepal.

pages.title: Functionalism: peace by pieces
pages.summary: Functionalism, based on the European Union experience and influenced by Cobden, rests on peace by pieces (low politics first, led by technicians and scientists), spill over effect leading to functional linkages, and functional sovereignty with decisions shifted to expert bodies. It transformed the nature of inter-state relations in the EU.

pages.title: Neo-functionalism and India-Pakistan composite dialogue
pages.summary: Functionalism may take extraordinarily long, and Ernst Haas's neo-functionalism says the process cannot be sustained without politicians, as EU integration stagnated without political will. In South Asia it appeared as the composite dialogue (2+6 framework) under the Vajpayee government, with short-term gains but vested interests making it hard to sustain, as after Mumbai.

pages.title: Democratic peace theory: Doyle's logic
pages.summary: Michael Doyle's theory says democracies do not go to war with each other, noting that wars in Europe happened under monarchies and autocracies. His logic is that people are treated as ends, free speech allows course correction, public opinion presses for peace, democracies promote tolerance, and they form a zone of peace.

pages.title: Democratic peace criticism and Bush Doctrine
pages.summary: The notes say more democracies are better for world peace, yet this is the most criticised theory, since the logic may be coincidence and free trade or common external threats may matter. Its worst aspect is legitimising US democracy promotion at gunpoint (Bush Doctrine, Iraq) and regime change, as China and Russia argue, while India has also promoted democracy in Nepal and Sri Lanka.

pages.title: India's democracy promotion; Pakistan's democracy
pages.summary: India joined the US-led Conference of Democracy and funds the UN democracy fund, but the notes advise Panchsheel-style non-interference in the neighbourhood because democracy lets parties play the China card, as in Maldives, Bhutan and Myanmar. On Pakistan there are two schools of thought, and India should not gesture in ways that make the army insecure.

flashcards.front: Which thinkers influenced the liberal school of International Politics and what did each contribute?
flashcards.back: Locke gave an enlightened view of human nature, and Kant's Perpetual Peace proposed free trade and republicanism. Cobden said to keep politicians out, and Norman Angell's The Great Illusion argued war is not beneficial even for victors.

flashcards.front: Why do the notes say liberal institutionalism cannot provide the alternative to realism?
flashcards.back: Institutions are used for narrow national interest, lack representativeness and transparency, lack funds, mandate and expertise, and countries trusting them have suffered, as India on Kashmir. Self-help remains relevant despite the UN.

flashcards.front: What are the contributions of Rosenau and John Burton to sociological liberalism?
flashcards.back: Rosenau says world order is becoming society-centric, with multiple identities and loyalties, global citizenship and transnationalism. Burton's cobweb model (against Wolfers' billiard ball model) shows the state is not the only gateway and its governability has declined.

flashcards.front: What is Karl Deutsch's security community and how does it emerge?
flashcards.back: It is an alternative to security dilemma, whose members feel common threats lie outside rather than threats to each other, as in Western Europe and North America. It emerges through communication, which he measured by travel, letters and phone calls.

flashcards.front: What are the three core concepts of functionalism?
flashcards.back: Peace by pieces, taking low politics first with technicians and scientists in the lead; the spill over effect, creating functional linkages; and functional sovereignty, shifting decisions from monistic sovereignty to expert bodies. It was applied in the European Union.

flashcards.front: How does neo-functionalism of Ernst Haas differ from functionalism?
flashcards.back: Haas says the process cannot be sustained without bringing in politicians, as EU integration stagnated when leaders lacked political will. The notes call it the strongest existing alternative to realist politics.

flashcards.front: What is the logic of Michael Doyle's democratic peace theory?
flashcards.back: Democracies do not fight each other because people are treated as ends, free speech allows course correction, public opinion presses for peace, and a culture of peace and tolerance forms a zone of peace.

flashcards.front: Why is democratic peace theory the most criticised liberal theory?
flashcards.back: Its logic may be coincidence, and factors like free trade or common external threat may explain peace. Its worst aspect is legitimising US democracy promotion at gunpoint (Bush Doctrine, Iraq) and regime change.

answers.question: Critically examine functionalism as a liberal approach to peace and discuss its relevance to India-Pakistan relations.
answers.intro: Functionalism, also called peace by pieces, is based on the European Union experience and influenced by Cobden's idea of keeping politicians out. It offers a liberal alternative to realist power politics by building cooperation step by step.
body: Peace by pieces separates issues into low politics and high politics, taking low politics first with technicians and scientists in the lead rather than political groups.

The spill over effect means that once nations see benefits of cooperation in one field they cooperate in others, building functional linkages that make resolving high politics conflicts easier. Functional sovereignty shifts decision making from monistic sovereignty to expert bodies. Applied in the European Union, this ultimately transformed the nature of inter-state relations.

Its limitation is extraordinary length, needing patience and political will. Ernst Haas's neo-functionalism says politicians cannot be left out, as EU integration stagnated until leaders showed will; the notes call it the strongest existing alternative to realism.

In South Asia it appeared as the composite dialogue (2+6 framework) under the Vajpayee government, with short-term gains, but vested interests acted, as at Mumbai, and made it hard to sustain. Margin notes mention the Gujral Doctrine's non-reciprocity.
answers.conclusion: Functionalism shows that cooperation on low politics can transform relations, as in the EU, but needs political will to survive. For India and Pakistan it remains worth trying, with the power of attraction rather than coercion.

answers.question: Democratic peace theory is among the most criticised liberal theories. Examine it and discuss whether democracy promotion should be India's aim in the neighbourhood.
answers.intro: Michael Doyle's democratic or republican peace theory holds that democracies do not go to war with each other, so more democracies mean better world peace. It is also the most criticised liberal theory, with implications for India's neighbourhood policy.
body: Doyle notes that wars in Europe occurred under monarchies and autocracies. His logic: people are treated as ends, free speech allows course correction, public opinion presses for peace, democracies promote tolerance and form a zone of peace.

Critics say the logic is insufficient and may be coincidence, and free trade or common external threat may explain peace. Its worst aspect is legitimising US democracy promotion at gunpoint (Bush Doctrine, Iraq), which China and Russia see as regime change.

India has promoted democracy in Nepal and Sri Lanka, joined the Conference of Democracy and funds the UN democracy fund. Yet the notes suggest Panchsheel-style non-interference, because democracy lets parties play the China card, as in Maldives and Bhutan, and promotion in Myanmar proved detrimental.

On Pakistan, army rule may bring stability, while real democracy would help through civil society; India should avoid gestures that make the army insecure and should not press the civilian government on issues outside its control.
answers.conclusion: Democratic peace theory offers an attractive logic but weak evidence and risky uses. For India, quiet support and non-interference are likely safer than active democracy promotion in a neighbourhood where parties can turn to rival powers.
